tier_reason: First-party numbers do exist (parser_benchmarks http/README.md and mp4/README.md, late-2013 MacBook Pro Core i7 2.3 GHz, exact CPU model not stated), but none is a valid win over a C baseline: idiomatic nom is slower than Joyent http-parser on all four HTTP tests, the nom-optimized edge over picohttpparser is within the error bars and pits Rust SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI code against a picohttpparser build whose SSE4.2 path the pico-sys default build compiles out (crippled-by-build-default precedent, AssemblyScript), and the 135x MP4 win over the C combinator library hammer measures different work on 2015 code (nom 0.1.6) that has since been rewritten. No valid measurement of a win stays at D.

corrections.baseline: Handwritten C HTTP parsers Joyent http-parser and h2o picohttpparser (parser_benchmarks/http); the MP4 benchmark compares against hammer (UpstandingHackers), a C parser-combinator library rather than a handwritten parser.
corrections.claimed_speedup: nom README: 'just as fast' as handwritten C parsers and 'often outperform ... even handwritten C parsers' (no numbers in nom's README). parser_benchmarks http/README.md (late-2013 MacBook Pro, quad-core 2.3 GHz Core i7): idiomatic nom is slower than Joyent http-parser on every test: 889 vs 606 ns one_test, 59,918 vs 56,385 ns small_test, 333,344 vs 266,254 ns bigger_test, 1,544 vs 1,137 ns httparse_example_test (1.06-1.47x slower, derived from page data). The SIMD 'nom (optimized)' experiment against picohttpparser: 183 vs 170 ns one_test (1.08x slower), 12,253 (+/- 2,473) vs 13,260 (+/- 1,786) ns small_test (1.08x faster), 61,519 (+/- 14,660) vs 65,415 (+/- 5,058) ns bigger_test (1.06x faster), 308 (+/- 48) vs 350 (+/- 76) ns httparse_example_test (1.14x faster) (ratios derived from page data; all within the error bars). mp4/README.md (2015, nom 0.1.6): nom 240 / 195 ns per iteration vs hammer 32,424 / 26,523 ns on small.mp4 / bigbuckbunny.mp4 with optimisations (about 135x, derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: HTTP run: compiler versions not stated. Joyent http-parser built with 'gcc -Ofast -O3 -DNDEBUG' (http/joyent_http_parser/Makefile) and timed by its own C clock_gettime loop; nom-http and nom-optimized (nom ^4.0) built with release profile lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1 and timed with the Rust bencher crate; nom-optimized README gives RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+sse2" (labelled SSE4.2; its take_while1_simd path emits PCMPESTRI); picohttpparser called via FFI from pico-sys 0.0.1, whose build.rs runs gcc::compile_library with crate defaults and no -msse4.2, so picohttpparser's __SSE4_2__ path is compiled out unless CFLAGS were set. MP4 run (2015): rustc 1.0.0-dev (522d09dfe 2015-02-19), nom 0.1.6, cargo bench; hammer at commit 4e8d319 built with Apple LLVM 6.0 (clang-600.0.56), scons --variant=opt, -Ofast -DNDEBUG, no -g.
corrections.hardware: Late-2013 MacBook Pro, quad-core 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7 (exact CPU model not stated)
corrections.workload: HTTP/1.x request parsing (one small request, the httparse example request, 55 requests in http-requests.txt, 275 requests in bigger.txt) against C parsers; MP4 top-level box parsing against the C combinator library hammer; JSON parsing compared only against Rust and other libraries (no C comparator).
corrections.caveats: The record said no numbers were openable; they are in parser_benchmarks http/README.md and mp4/README.md, and they do not support a win over C. (1) Idiomatic nom loses to Joyent http-parser on all four HTTP tests even though the C harness mallocs and memcpys every header name and value while nom returns borrowed slices; the two sides also use different timing harnesses (Rust bencher vs a C clock_gettime loop that drops the seconds field). (2) The nom-optimized edge over picohttpparser (1.06-1.14x on three tests, 1.08x slower on one_test) is inside the stated error bars and is asymmetric: nom-optimized uses SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI range scans while pico-sys 0.0.1 compiles picohttpparser without -msse4.2, disabling its own SSE4.2 path (crippled baseline by build default). (3) The MP4 135x over hammer is not a handwritten C parser and not the same work: the hammer harness parses every box body as per-byte h_uint8 tokens through h_length_value with arena allocation and treats the MP4 size field (which includes the 8-byte header) as the body length, so it appears to over-read and stop after the first box, while nom slices box bodies; the table comes from nom 0.1.6 on a pre-1.0 rustc (2015) and the checked-in nom-mp4 code is now nom 5 with jemalloc, so the numbers are not reproducible from current code. (4) The README's own wording is parity ('just as fast'). parser_benchmarks last commit 2019-12-10, 128 stars, no LICENSE shown. Kept for notability (10.5k stars, about 785 million crates.io downloads).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 10.5k stars, 849 forks; about 785 million crates.io downloads (crates.io API, 2026-10-12); latest release 8.0.0 (2025-01-26)
corrections.why_faster: Where nom is ahead, the sources point to non-language causes: nom-optimized's take_while1_simd uses SSE4.2 PCMPESTRI for URI and header-value scans against a picohttpparser build with its SSE4.2 path compiled out; against hammer, nom returns zero-copy borrowed slices per box while hammer's generic backend builds an arena-allocated token per byte and pays per-parse setup. Idiomatic nom without SIMD is slower than Joyent http-parser.

notes: Tier stays D, but the record's 'numbers not found' caveat is wrong: parser_benchmarks http/ and mp4/ READMEs carry first-party tables. Shortcomings to record: idiomatic nom 1.06-1.47x slower than Joyent http-parser (derived); nom-optimized vs picohttpparser within noise and SIMD-asymmetric (pico-sys default build drops picohttpparser's SSE4.2 path); hammer MP4 comparison measures different work on 2015 nom 0.1.6 code. Metadata checked: MIT (LICENSE file), not archived, not a fork, last commit 2025-08-26 'Fix for issue 1808 (#1811)', about 13.5 months old, so 'stale' is correct.
